sn46.1:1.2.pli: “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, himavantaṃ pabbatarājānaṃ nissāya nāgā kāyaṃ vaḍḍhenti, balaṃ gāhenti;
sn46.1:1.2.eng: “Mendicants, dragons grow and wax strong supported by the Himalayas, the king of mountains.
sn46.1:1.2.comm: For the “dragon” (nāga) see SN 29.1:1.1 and notes. | The etymological root of nāga seems to be “naked” (Pali nagga), from where it was applied to hairless animals such as the “snake”, especially the cobra, and the elephant. It is also connected with that naked feature of the earth, the mountain (naga). That which belongs to the mountain is the nāga, the “dragon”; the primordial serpent Vṛtra coiled around the mountain (SN 2.3:3.4). Nāga is also a term for hill tribes. The snake, elephant, and mountain are all powerful, and their nakedness emphasizes their independence. This, it seems, informed the cluster of meanings behind applying nāga to the shaven-headed and spiritually mighty “giants”, the arahants.

sn46.1:1.3.pli: te tattha kāyaṃ vaḍḍhetvā balaṃ gāhetvā kusobbhe otaranti, kusobbhe otaritvā mahāsobbhe otaranti, mahāsobbhe otaritvā kunnadiyo otaranti, kunnadiyo otaritvā mahānadiyo otaranti, mahānadiyo otaritvā mahāsamuddasāgaraṃ otaranti; te tattha mahantattaṃ vepullattaṃ āpajjanti kāyena;
sn46.1:1.3.eng: When they’re strong they dive into the pools. Then they dive into the lakes, the streams, the rivers, and finally the ocean. There they acquire a great and abundant body.

sn46.1:1.4.pli: evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya satta bojjhaṅge bhāvento satta bojjhaṅge bahulīkaronto mahantattaṃ vepullattaṃ pāpuṇāti dhammesu.
sn46.1:1.4.eng: In the same way, a mendicant develops and cultivates the seven awakening factors depending on and grounded on ethics, acquiring great and abundant good qualities.
sn46.1:1.4.comm: The seven awakening factors especially emphasize the emotional and holistic dimension of meditative growth. Unlike the eightfold path, they do not explicitly include the factor of ethics, but this passage shows that ethics is their foundation. See also, eg. SN 46.6.

sn46.1:1.5.pli: Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya satta bojjhaṅge bhāvento satta bojjhaṅge bahulīkaronto mahantattaṃ vepullattaṃ pāpuṇāti dhammesūti?
sn46.1:1.5.eng: And how does a mendicant develop the seven awakening factors depending on and grounded on ethics, acquiring great and abundant good qualities?

sn46.1:1.6.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ;
sn46.1:1.6.eng: It’s when a mendicant develops the awakening factor of mindfulness, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go.
sn46.1:1.6.comm: The factors of mindfulness and investigation of principles both have a dual meaning in this context. They can refer to “bringing to mind” and “investigating” the principles or phenomena experienced in meditation. But they can also refer to recalling the “teaching” and reflecting on it (SN 46.3).

sn46.1:1.7.eng: They develop the awakening factor of investigation of principles …
sn46.1:1.7.comm: Dhamma means the “principle” of cause and effect, as in “observation of principles” (dhammānupassanā), “investigation of principles” (dhammavicaya), or “discernment of principles” (dhammavipassanā).

sn46.1:1.8.eng: They develop the awakening factor of energy …

sn46.1:1.9.eng: They develop the awakening factor of rapture …
sn46.1:1.9.comm: “Rapture” (pīti) is a joyous emotional response to pleasure, usually a spiritual sense of elevation or uplift in meditation.

sn46.1:1.10.eng: They develop the awakening factor of tranquility …
sn46.1:1.10.comm: “Tranquility” (passaddhi) is a settled and serene body and mind, as activities or energies become stilled through the process of meditation.

sn46.1:1.11.eng: They develop the awakening factor of immersion …

sn46.1:1.12.pli: upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ.
sn46.1:1.12.eng: They develop the awakening factor of equanimity, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go.
sn46.1:1.12.comm: “Equanimity” (upekkhā) of the fourth absorption and above, or else the equanimity of insight (MN 152).

sn46.1:1.13.pli: Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sīlaṃ nissāya sīle patiṭṭhāya satta bojjhaṅge bhāvento satta bojjhaṅge bahulīkaronto mahantattaṃ vepullattaṃ pāpuṇāti dhammesū”ti.
sn46.1:1.13.eng: That’s how a mendicant develops and cultivates the seven awakening factors depending on and grounded on ethics, acquiring great and abundant good qualities.”

sn46.10:1.1.pli: “Sattime, bhikkhave, bojjhaṅgā bhāvitā bahulīkatā anuppannā uppajjanti, nāññatra sugatavinayā.
sn46.10:1.1.eng: “Mendicants, these seven awakening factors don’t arise to be developed and cultivated apart from the Holy One’s training.

sn46.10:1.3.eng: The awakening factors of mindfulness, investigation of principles, energy, rapture, tranquility, immersion, and equanimity.

sn46.10:1.4.pli: ime kho, bhikkhave, satta bojjhaṅgā bhāvitā bahulīkatā anuppannā uppajjanti, nāññatra sugatavinayā”ti.
sn46.10:1.4.eng: These seven awakening factors don’t arise to be developed and cultivated apart from the Holy One’s training.”

sn46.11:1.1.pli: “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ye keci pāṇā cattāro iriyāpathe kappenti—

sn46.111-120:1.3.eng: The search for sensual pleasures, the search for continued existence, and the search for a spiritual path. …”

sn46.12:1.1.pli: “Sūriyassa, bhikkhave, udayato etaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ etaṃ pubbanimittaṃ, yadidaṃ—aruṇuggaṃ;
sn46.12:1.1.eng: “Mendicants, the dawn is the forerunner and harbinger of the sunrise.

sn46.12:1.2.pli: evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno sattannaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ uppādāya etaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ etaṃ nimittaṃ, yadidaṃ—kalyāṇamittatā.
sn46.12:1.2.eng: In the same way, for a mendicant good friendship is the forerunner and harbinger of the arising of the seven awakening factors.

sn46.12:1.3.pli: Kalyāṇamittassetaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno pāṭikaṅkhaṃ—satta bojjhaṅge bhāvessati, satta bojjhaṅge bahulīkarissati.
sn46.12:1.3.eng: A mendicant with good friends can expect to develop and cultivate the seven awakening factors.

sn46.12:2.1.pli: Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kalyāṇamitto satta bojjhaṅge bhāveti satta bojjhaṅge bahulīkaroti?

sn46.12:2.2.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ …pe…

sn46.12:2.3.pli: upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ.

sn46.12:2.4.pli: Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kalyāṇamitto satta bojjhaṅge bhāveti, satta bojjhaṅge bahulīkarotī”ti.

sn46.13:1.1.pli: “Sūriyassa, bhikkhave, udayato etaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ etaṃ pubbanimittaṃ, yadidaṃ—aruṇuggaṃ;

sn46.130:1.4.eng: Desire for rebirth in the realm of luminous form, desire for rebirth in the formless realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.

sn46.130:1.5.eng: These are the five higher fetters.

sn46.130:1.6.pli: Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, pañcannaṃ uddhambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ abhiññāya pariññāya parikkhayāya pahānāya satta bojjhaṅgā bhāvetabbā.
sn46.130:1.6.eng: The seven awakening factors should be developed for the direct knowledge, complete understanding, finishing, and giving up of these five higher fetters.

sn46.130:1.8.pli: Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ …pe…
sn46.130:1.8.eng: It’s when a mendicant develops the awakening factors of mindfulness, investigation of principles, energy, rapture, tranquility, immersion,

sn46.130:1.9.eng: and equanimity, which culminate in the removal of greed, hate, and delusion. …”

sn46.130:1.10.eng: “… which have freedom from death as their objective, destination, and culmination …”

sn46.130:1.11.eng: “… which slant, slope, and incline to extinguishment …

sn46.130:1.12.pli: Imesaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pañcannaṃ uddhambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ abhiññāya pariññāya parikkhayāya pahānāya ime satta bojjhaṅgā bhāvetabbā”ti.
sn46.130:1.12.eng: The seven awakening factors should be developed for the direct knowledge, complete understanding, finishing, and giving up of these five higher fetters.”

sn46.14:1.1.eng: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground.

sn46.14:1.2.pli: Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā mahākassapo pippaliguhāyaṃ viharati ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno.
sn46.14:1.2.eng: Now at that time Venerable Mahākassapa was staying in the Pipphali cave, and he was sick, suffering, gravely ill.

sn46.14:1.3.pli: Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā mahākassapo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Nisajja kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ mahākassapaṃ etadavoca:
sn46.14:1.3.eng: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of retreat, went to Venerable Mahākassapa, sat down on the seat spread out, and said to him:

sn46.14:2.1.pli: “Kacci te, kassapa, khamanīyaṃ kacci yāpanīyaṃ? Kacci dukkhā vedanā paṭikkamanti, no abhikkamanti; paṭikkamosānaṃ paññāyati, no abhikkamo”ti?
sn46.14:2.1.eng: “I hope you’re keeping well, Kassapa; I hope you’re all right. And I hope the pain is fading, not growing, that its fading is evident, not its growing.”

sn46.14:2.2.pli: “Na me, bhante, khamanīyaṃ, na yāpanīyaṃ. Bāḷhā me dukkhā vedanā abhikkamanti, no paṭikkamanti; abhikkamosānaṃ paññāyati, no paṭikkamo”ti.
sn46.14:2.2.eng: “Sir, I’m not keeping well, I’m not getting by. The pain is terrible and growing, not fading; its growing is evident, not its fading.”
sn46.14:2.2.comm: Accurately reporting symptoms is a characteristic of a good patient (AN 5.123).

sn46.14:3.1.pli: “Sattime, kassapa, bojjhaṅgā mayā sammadakkhātā bhāvitā bahulīkatā abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattanti.
sn46.14:3.1.eng: “Kassapa, I’ve rightly explained these seven awakening factors. When developed and cultivated, they lead to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to extinguishment.

sn46.14:3.3.pli: Satisambojjhaṅgo kho, kassapa, mayā sammadakkhāto bhāvito bahulīkato abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati …pe… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo kho, kassapa, mayā sammadakkhāto bhāvito bahulīkato abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati.
sn46.14:3.3.eng: The awakening factors of mindfulness, investigation of principles, energy, rapture, tranquility, immersion, and equanimity.

sn46.14:3.4.pli: Ime kho, kassapa, satta bojjhaṅgā mayā sammadakkhātā bhāvitā bahulīkatā abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattantī”ti.
sn46.14:3.4.eng: These are the seven awakening factors that I’ve rightly explained. When developed and cultivated, they lead to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to extinguishment.”

sn46.14:3.5.eng: “Indeed, Blessed One, these are awakening factors!

sn46.14:3.6.eng: Indeed, Holy One, these are awakening factors!”

sn46.14:4.1.eng: That is what the Buddha said.

sn46.14:4.2.pli: Attamano āyasmā mahākassapo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandi.
sn46.14:4.2.eng: Satisfied, Venerable Mahākassapa approved what the Buddha said.

sn46.14:4.3.eng: And that’s how he recovered from that illness.
sn46.14:4.3.comm: This discourse and the next two are included in the Sinhalese Maha Pirit Pota. Monks often recite them for recovery from illness. In Thailand, a set of verses known as the Bojjhaṅga-paritta are recited.

sn46.14:4.4.pli: Tathāpahīno cāyasmato mahākassapassa so ābādho ahosīti.
